extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media scholars, journalism students, and the general public interested in news selection
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and factors used by journalists and editors to decide which events become news and how stories are presented. Covers both event-related values (e.g., timeliness, proximity) and process-related values (e.g., continuity, composition, shareability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that occur suddenly and fit well with the news organisation's schedule are more likely to be reported than those that occur gradually or at inconvenient times of day or night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term trends are less likely to receive coverage; immediacy and fit with production schedules make items more usable for newsrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that have only just happened, are current, ongoing, or are about to happen are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recency increases selection probability; being current or imminent makes an event attractive to editors and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity / Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: To do with people or places close to the target audience; includes geographical and cultural proximity (sometimes called meaningfulness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local or culturally proximate events are more immediately understandable and relevant to audiences, increasing coverage likelihood; cultural proximity (shared language, appearance, preoccupations) raises newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad news (disasters, crime, adverse developments) is more newsworthy than good news; often described as 'the basic news value.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negativity tends to drive coverage and placement; however, positivity can be a news value in contexts such as sports or feel‑good stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity
rubrics_metrics.description: In some contexts (e.g., sports, science, feel‑good tabloid stories) positive developments are considered newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positivity sometimes operates alongside or instead of negativity depending on genre and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition of people or forces resulting in a dramatic effect; events involving disagreement, tension or opposition are highly newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict (wars, protests, political fights) often leads to extensive coverage and repeated updates; it can shape presentation and allow persuasive framing in political stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are out of the ordinary, unexpected, or rare are more newsworthy than routine or unsurprising events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel or surprising elements increase interest; however this can interact with consonance (readiness to report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events whose implications are clear make for better copy than those open to multiple interpretations or requiring complex background to understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that are straightforward to explain are favoured because they make clearer, more accessible news items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that can be portrayed as the actions of individuals are more attractive than those without a human-interest element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualising issues through specific people (ordinary individuals rather than abstract masses) increases audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness / Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Relates to the audience's sense of identification with the topic: cultural proximity and relevance to readers' own lives increase newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance is assessed by how close an event or change is to the experiences or concerns of the target audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: An event's significance or consequences (for the target audience or others); events with significant consequences (high impact) are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-impact events (large numbers affected, major policy implications) attract editorial attention and higher placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence / Eliteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events involving high-status people, global powers, celebrities, the rich or powerful are more likely to be reported (also refers to eliteness of sources/attribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominent actors increase recognisability and audience interest; prominence can interact with other values (e.g., a conflict involving notable figures is more newsworthy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Superlativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events with a large scale, scope or high intensity (e.g., 'largest', 'worst') are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extreme or record-holding characteristics make stories stand out (scale, scope, intensity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that fit with the media's expectations, stereotypes, or mental scripts receive more coverage than those that defy them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consonance refers to the media's readiness to report an item; it can conflict with unexpectedness, but really describes editorial preparedness and fit with existing narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: A story already in the news gathers inertia because organisations are already set up to report it and earlier reportage makes it more accessible to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing stories are easier to update and therefore more likely to receive continued coverage; previous investment (resources, audience interest) sustains attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories must compete for space; editors seek a balance of types of coverage so prominence depends on a story's own values and those of competing stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement and prominence are influenced by the need to compose a balanced program/edition; oversupply in one area can push stories down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial or professional competition between media may lead journalists to adopt or amplify the news value given to a story by a rival outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rival coverage can elevate a marginal item into broader attention; newsrooms may follow competitors' lead to avoid missing stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-option
rubrics_metrics.description: A story only marginally newsworthy on its own may be covered if it is related to a major running story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linking small items to big narratives increases their chance of being published (e.g., tying local incidents to national scandals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: A marginal story that is already written and available may be selected ahead of a more newsworthy story that requires fresh research and writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handy pre-written copy can displace more important but time-consuming reporting because of resource constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: An event is more likely to be covered if it has been pre-scheduled (predictable events are easier to plan coverage for).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scheduled events (elections, press conferences) benefit from logistical planning and are therefore more likely to be covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story impact / Shareability
rubrics_metrics.description: The impact of the published story itself—whether it is being shared widely, read, liked, or commented on—affects editorial decisions in the modern news environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytics and social metrics (shareability) mean that stories that are simple, emotional, unexpected and triggered may be prioritised; engagement metrics are now an important part of newsroom practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional news media have strict deadlines and short production cycles, selecting for items that can be researched and covered quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that can be turned around rapidly are favoured; tight schedules can limit in-depth coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to deploy and control reporting staff and technical resources (and the functionality of these resources) can determine whether a story is covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical barriers (transport, communications, staff availability) influence selection despite an event's theoretical newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data / Facticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Media need to back up stories with data to remain relevant and reliable; reporters prefer raw data for an unbiased perspective (also called facticity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability of verifiable facts and figures strengthens a story's credibility and increases its likelihood of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience relevance / Security concern
rubrics_metrics.description: From the audience perspective, news value is determined by degree of change and the relevance of that change to individuals or groups; items that threaten peace, prosperity or wellbeing act as risk signals and are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and communicators may manipulate perceived relevance ('security concern') to expand or contract the boundary of relevance for audiences; relevance declines with distance from individuals to family, social group, society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Usefulness Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptions of newsworthiness can be contaminated by political usefulness bias—people tend to view stories that provide 'ammunition' for their political views as more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a cognitive/political influence on selection and perception; it explains why some audiences or journalists might prioritise stories that support their positions.
